header.what: What French can and cannot do with sounds, and which of its words it will not put on a card. The rules live in the engine; this file is what makes them French.
header.cannotStart: French has no /h/ phoneme at all, so hôtel is said without one; it has no /ɸ/, and no native onset for the two affricates. An anchor claiming one of these matches only on paper.
header.anchors: What an anchor of this language may be. How far a word may sit from a reading and still be heard in it, how far two anchors must sit from each other, what an unrated word is worth against a rated one, how many morae a reading may run to before no one word carries it, how common a word must be before a reader is likely to know it, which parts of speech a story can be built on, and how many words a cue carries before it is a sentence rather than a thing. The unrated value is the middle of the scale the ratings use, which runs from 0 to 100 here: nothing rated the word, and that is evidence neither way.
header.hears: What a French ear reaches for on hearing a Japanese sound French does not make. A substitution brings one sound onto another and never two onto one, nor onto a sound a reading already carries: hearing chi as the sound of chic would give it shi's onset, and hearing tsu as /s/ would give it su's, and a reader handed the word would produce one of the two and be graded on the other. So those two keep no substitution and their readings keep no anchor.
header.writes: A sound French does not say and does write. A reading beginning on one is compared from the sound that follows it, and its anchor has to be spelled with the letter stated here: la hache is said without an h and carries one where the reader looks, and a mnemonic is read. cannotStart has nothing to say about it, that rule refusing a pronunciation claiming a sound French does not make, which a pronunciation derived from the lexicon cannot do.
header.refuses: Words a card will not carry, whatever they sound like. Neither frequency nor distance catches these: shit is an ordinary noun of the lexicon and stood for shi, one of the readings a learner meets first. The list grows as a reading is read and refused, the way the component names grew.
